source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Expected early satiety is the best explanation for severe persistent pain that radiates to the back.","B":"Acute pancreatitis should be suspected when severe persistent abdominal pain may radiate to the back, with or without vomiting.","C":"Injection-site irritation typically causes severe upper-abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting.","D":"Isolated hypoglycemia characteristically presents as persistent abdominal pain radiating to the back."}}
source_row.rationale: GLP-1 receptor agonist labeling warns about acute pancreatitis. Persistent severe abdominal pain, sometimes radiating to the back and accompanied by nausea or vomiting, warrants prompt evaluation rather than being treated as an expected gastrointestinal effect.
source_row.source_detail: Warnings and Precautions §5.2 — Acute Pancreatitis; characteristic severe persistent abdominal pain, sometimes radiating to the back. Current 2026 DailyMed/FDA labeling; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring, reconciliation and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
source_row.stem: A client using a GLP-1 receptor agonist reports persistent severe abdominal pain that may radiate to the back, with nausea and vomiting. Which adverse effect should the nurse suspect?
